Python and Julia chunks

Source: vignettes/languages.Rmd
languages.Rmd

This article is for authors who compute with Python or Julia and want weft’s values and checks in the prose around that code. It assumes you know vignette("values", package = "weft") and vignette("wording", package = "weft"). After it you will be able to print a Python or Julia value in a sentence, govern wording with it, call weft’s formatters from Python, and know what weft checks in such a document and what it cannot check. For a document that is not knit, see vignette("named-values", package = "weft").

The chunks in this article need Python or Julia, so most of them are not run when the article is built. The output shown was produced by running them.

What works and where

weft is an R package that works inside knitr. A document with Python or Julia chunks works when knitr knits it: an .Rmd, or a Quarto .qmd with engine: knitr in its front matter. R is installed and runs the render. Python chunks run through the R package reticulate, and Julia chunks through the R package JuliaCall. The prose is still R: a Python or Julia value reaches a sentence through an R expression.

For a Quarto author this means one line in the front matter:

---
title: "River survey"
engine: knitr
---

A .qmd that Quarto runs with its Jupyter or Julia engine has no R to evaluate prose, so an R expression in it is not evaluated and prints as text. Such a document can still use weft: write a value by name, `depth`{.num}, publish it from the Python or Julia code, and weft’s Pandoc filter fills it in. That route is described in vignette("named-values", package = "weft"). Everything below is for documents that knitr knits.

Setting up

You need:

  • for Python chunks, the R package reticulate and a Python it can find;
  • for Julia chunks, Julia, the R package JuliaCall, and the Julia package RCall that JuliaCall uses;
  • weft turned on in the document, as for any weft document (see vignette("setup", package = "weft")).

Prose needs no library(reticulate) and no library(JuliaCall). weft_setup() loads neither, and starts neither Python nor Julia. A document with no Python or Julia in it never loads them.

weft never installs Python, Julia or a package for either. To choose a Python, set RETICULATE_PYTHON in your .Renviron. When weft starts Python itself and RETICULATE_USE_MANAGED_VENV is not set, it sets it to no for that start, so reticulate does not download a Python of its own. R code of yours that starts Python first follows reticulate’s own rules. For Julia, run JuliaCall::julia_setup() once by hand: it installs RCall. weft starts Julia with installJulia = FALSE and install = FALSE, so it installs nothing.

Python chunks must run through reticulate’s engine, knitr’s default. With the chunk option python.reticulate = FALSE each chunk is a separate Python process, and weft cannot read its values.

A Python value in a sentence

Write a Python value in prose as reticulate’s documentation does: `r py$depth`. Every weft construct takes it.

---
title: "River survey"
output: md_document
knitr:
  opts_knit:
    weft: !expr weft::weft_setup()
---

```{python survey}
depth = 3.14159
visits = 12
sites = ['Upper', 'Lower', 'Weir']
flagged = ['Weir']
rising = True
```

Mean depth was `r py$depth`{.num} m at `r py$sites`{.and}.
We made `r py$visits`{.word} visits, and
[no site was | # was | # were]{list="py$flagged"} flagged.
Turbidity [rose | fell]{if="py$rising"} over the year.
The deepest reading was `r claim(py$depth, . < 5)`{.num} m.

renders as:

Mean depth was 3.1 m at Upper, Lower and Weir. We made twelve visits,
and Weir was flagged. Turbidity rose over the year. The deepest reading
was 3.1 m.

claim(py$depth, . < 5) is a check, as in any weft document. In a Quarto document the value is written `{r} py$depth`{.num}.

Why weft reads Python values itself

A Python integer can be any size. R holds whole numbers exactly only up to 2^53, about 9 × 10^15. reticulate converts a Python value to an R value in its compiled code, before any R code sees it, and for some large integers the result is a wrong number with no error. 2**53 + 1 arrives in R as 1. Once it is 1, nothing can tell it from a right 1.

So in every expression weft evaluates (a value, a bare value, a governor, a caption on an R chunk, a string given to weft_str()), weft reads py$name, py[["name"]] and chains such as py$cfg$depth itself. It reads the Python object, decides its kind from its Python type, and refuses a value that R cannot hold exactly:

```{python count}
particles = 2**53 + 1
```

```{r compare}
reticulate::py$particles
```

The filter caught `r py$particles`{.num} particles.

The R chunk shows what reticulate’s conversion gives:

reticulate::py$particles
## [1] 1

The sentence does not print “1”. The render fails with:

weft: 1 failure
  count.Rmd:17  [value error] `r py$particles`
      `py$particles` is the Python int 9007199254740993, beyond ±2^53, where R cannot hold a whole number exactly. Scale it in Python, or bind str() of it and print the text (rule 2.12.5).

What R does with the value after weft has read it is R’s: `r length(py$sites)` and `r py$slope > 0` work as they would on an R vector. If an R chunk binds an object called py, prose reads that object, not Python. A call such as py$f(2) is reticulate’s, unchanged.

What each Python type becomes

The kind comes from the Python type, never from how the value prints.

Python In R
True, False, numpy.bool_ TRUE, FALSE
int and numpy integers, up to 2^31 − 1 in size an integer
the same, from 2^31 to 2^53 in size a double, exact
the same, beyond 2^53 refused
float and numpy floats a double
decimal.Decimal, up to 15 significant digits the nearest double
decimal.Decimal, more digits refused: round it with quantize()
str a string
datetime.date, numpy.datetime64 in days a Date
datetime.datetime, pandas.Timestamp refused: convert with .date()
list, tuple, a one-dimensional numpy array, pandas.Series a vector
dict whose keys are all str a vector with names, in the dict’s order
set, frozenset refused: bind sorted() of it
a numpy array of two or more dimensions refused
anything else (complex, bytes, fractions.Fraction, pandas.DataFrame, an object of your own class) refused

A bool is never read as a number, though Python’s bool is a kind of int.

A list is read element by element. Its elements must be of one kind, with two mixes allowed: integers with floats make floats, and integers with decimals make decimals. [1, 'a'] is refused, and so is a list that holds a list:

`py$mixed` is a Python list whose elements are of more than one kind (integer, string); weft reads a list whose elements are all of one kind (rule 1.11.4).
`py$nested` is a Python list that holds a list; weft reads a flat list (rule 1.11.4).

A refusal found on one element names it: “Element 2 of `py$x` is a Python datetime.datetime, …”.

Missing values

These Python values are missing: None, a float NaN or infinity (numpy’s too), Decimal('NaN') and Decimal('Infinity'), pandas.NA, pandas.NaT and numpy.datetime64('NaT'). A missing element of a list is allowed anywhere: [3, None, 5] is c(3L, NA, 5L).

A missing value given to a formatter or a governor is a “no value” failure, as an R NA is. A bare `r py$gap` with gap = None prints “NA”. An empty list is not missing: it is a list of length zero, and the rules for length zero apply (vignette("values", package = "weft")).

Conditions are bools

Python treats [], 0 and '' as false in an if. weft does not. When an if condition is exactly one Python read, the value must be a bool. Anything else is a value error, not false, because a sentence chosen by an accident of truthiness is a wrong sentence:

```{python flags}
flagged = []
has_flags = len(flagged) > 0
```

[Some sites were | No site was]{if="py$flagged"} flagged.
[Some sites were | No site was]{if="py$has_flags"} flagged.
[Some sites were | No site was]{if="length(py$flagged) > 0"} flagged.
weft: 1 failure
  truth.Rmd:14  [value error] "Some sites were"
      `py$flagged` is a Python list; an `if` condition must be a bool (rule 1.11.8).

The second and third lines print “No site was flagged.”. Write the test in Python, as has_flags does, or in R, as the third line does. The same holds for the other governors: an n or sign governor that is exactly one Python read must be a number (a list of one number is not), and a list span needs a list.

Python values in R code

In an R chunk, py$x is reticulate’s conversion: weft does not rewrite R chunk code. To read a value in R code by the same rules as prose, use py_value(). Each argument is one step of a path: a name, then a key of a dict or an attribute.

```{python fit}
means = {'Upper': 1.25, 'Lower': 3.4}
```

```{r in-r}
py_value("means")
py_value("means", "Upper")
```
py_value("means")
## Upper Lower
##  1.25  3.40
py_value("means", "Upper")
## [1] 1.25

py_value() works at the console too, and needs no library(reticulate). A pandas DataFrame for a plot is still reticulate’s to convert: py_value() refuses a table, because a table has no place in a sentence.

Formatting from Python

weft’s function forms are a Python module, weft, while a document is knitted. Import from it as from any module:

```{python labels}
from weft import fmt_num, fmt_and, plural
print(fmt_num(3.14159))
print(fmt_and(['Upper', 'Lower', 'Weir']))
print(plural(3, "# site", "# sites"))
try:
    fmt_num(2**53 + 1)
except Exception as e:
    print(e)
print(r.fmt_num(2**53 + 1))
```
## 3.1
## Upper, Lower and Weir
## 3 sites
## Argument 1 of fmt_num() is the Python int 9007199254740993, beyond ±2^53, where R cannot hold a whole number exactly. Scale it in Python, or bind str() of it and print the text (rule 2.12.5).
## 1

Each function returns what the R function of that name returns: one string as a str, several as a list of str. Its arguments are read by the rules above, so fmt_num(2**53 + 1) raises an exception with weft’s message.

The last line shows why r.fmt_num() is a lint finding. reticulate’s r object hands the Python arguments to R through the same conversion, and 2**53 + 1 arrives as 1.

The module holds fmt_num, fmt_pct, fmt_sci, fmt_p, fmt_date, fmt_no, fmt_word, fmt_count, fmt_ord, fmt_and, fmt_or, fmt_pairs, fmt_range, fmt_ul, fmt_ol, fmt_dl, fmt_a, fmt_cap, fmt_strong, fmt_em, plural, ci, pm, about, of_n and weft_str. The module also holds claim, put and auto: claim(n, "> 10") checks in Python where it runs, and put() and auto() publish names for the filter (see vignette("named-values", package = "weft")). u, fmt_unit, lookup, brk and the dictionary functions are not there. A check on a value in prose is still written in R, as `r claim(py$n, . > 10)`. If a module called weft is already loaded in Python, weft leaves it in place and warns once.

Text with constructs from Python

Text a Python chunk prints with results = "asis" is not resolved by weft. To print a sentence with constructs from Python, pass it through weft_str() from the module. The expressions inside the markup are R, so they read Python values with py$:

```{python summary, results = "asis"}
from weft import weft_str
print(weft_str('Turbidity [rose | fell]{if="py$slope > 0"} over the year.'))
```
Turbidity rose over the year.

A check that fails inside it is collected, located by the chunk’s label, and fails the render once at the end.

Captions

weft resolves a caption written in an R chunk’s options (see vignette("values", package = "weft")), but not one written in a Python or Julia chunk’s options. A construct there is a construct error, found by the lints and at knit time. A named value does work in any caption (see vignette("named-values", package = "weft")). In a Quarto document that knitr knits, write the caption in a figure or table div instead, where it is prose:

::: {#fig-depth}
```{python depth-plot}
plot_depths()
```

Depth at [one site | # sites]{n="py$n_sites"}.
:::

Warnings and errors

Every warning Python shows while a document is knitted goes into the document’s condition log, as an R warning does (see vignette("gate", package = "weft")). It still prints where it printed before. For a chunk model that runs warnings.warn("fit did not converge"), the log holds:

{"from":"chunk","source":"model","class":"warning","normalised":"UserWarning: fit did not converge","text":"UserWarning: fit did not converge"}

A Python exception in a chunk with error = TRUE is logged too, with class error and text such as ValueError: no readings for Weir. Without error = TRUE the knit stops, as it does without weft. A chunk served from knitr’s cache replays the conditions it logged when it ran.

The severity list in _weft.yml applies to Python warnings. With severity: ["did not converge"] the same document fails the render:

weft: 1 failure
  fit.Rmd chunk model  [condition]
      warning: UserWarning: fit did not converge
      matched the severity pattern did not converge

Not logged: text a chunk prints to sys.stderr, output of Python’s logging module, and warnings that a warnings filter hides.

Files the document read

The ledger’s header records the files a document read, with a hash of each (see vignette("gate", package = "weft")). A Python module whose file lies inside the project, and that is loaded when the knit ends, is one of them. With import trend in a chunk and trend.py beside the document:

{"weft":"ledger","version":1,"source":"fit.Rmd","output":"fit","dict":{},"files":{"fit.Rmd":"fed61ddb49d8fa42","trend.py":"5dc4f531ced53f1e"},"targets":{}}

Edit trend.py and the document’s values are listed as not re-rendered until it is rendered again. Modules under site-packages, a virtual environment, renv or a folder whose name starts with . are left out. A literal path given to reticulate::source_python() or reticulate::py_run_file() in an R chunk is recorded too. Data files that Python reads, such as a CSV given to pandas.read_csv(), are not, as for R.

The lints

The static lints read a Python or Julia document as they read any other (see vignette("lints", package = "weft")). Code rules read R chunks only, so a Python chunk that assigns dict or reads tar_read gives no finding. Four rules are about other languages:

Id Tier Finds What to do
guest-inline 1 inline code in another language, such as `{python} depth`, which knitr prints as code bind the value to a name in a chunk and write `r py$depth` or `r jl_value("depth")`
guest-call 1 r.fmt_num() and the other function forms called from Python through reticulate’s r object from weft import fmt_num; a claim() belongs in prose
guest-read 2 py$x in R chunk code, and a reticulate or JuliaCall call (py_eval(), julia_eval()) in an expression weft evaluates read the value with py_value() or jl_value(); leave a data frame for a plot as it is
ojs-value 2 an Observable value in prose see “Observable JS” below

This project has one .Rmd with each kind of mistake, and a .qmd set to run with Jupyter:

library(weft)
writeLines("", "_weft.yml")
writeLines(c(
  "---",
  "title: \"Depths\"",
  "---",
  "",
  "```{python depths}",
  "depth = 3.14159",
  "label = r.fmt_num(depth)",
  "```",
  "",
  "```{python depth-plot}",
  "#| fig-cap: |",
  "#|   Depth at [one site | # sites]{n=\"k\"}.",
  "#| fig-alt: \"Depth by site.\"",
  "plot_depths()",
  "```",
  "",
  "```{r plot-data}",
  "d <- py$depth",
  "```",
  "",
  "Mean depth was `{python} depth` m.",
  "Mean depth was `r py_eval(\"depth\")`{.num} m."
), "depths.Rmd")
writeLines(c(
  "---",
  "title: \"Report\"",
  "jupyter: python3",
  "---",
  "",
  "```{python}",
  "#| label: count",
  "n = 12",
  "```",
  "",
  "We visited [one site | # sites]{n=\"n\"}."
), "report.qmd")
lints(tier = 1:2)
#> weft lints: 6 findings in 2 files (4 tier 1, 2 tier 2)
#> 
#> depths.Rmd
#>   7:9    guest-call    `r.fmt_num()` passes its arguments through reticulate, which can turn a Python int into a wrong number with no error. Write `from weft import fmt_num` and call `fmt_num()` (rule 5.11.2).
#>   12:15  construct     A `n` construct in a caption of chunk `depth-plot`, which uses the `python` engine, not R: write the caption in a figure or table div instead, `::: {#fig-name}` ... caption paragraph ... `:::` (rules 1.10.5, 2.3.5).
#>   18:6   guest-read    `py$depth` in R code is converted by reticulate, which can turn a Python int into a wrong number with no error. For a value that reaches prose, read it with py_value("depth") (rule 5.11.3).
#>   21:16  guest-inline  `{python} depth` is inline Python, which the knitr engine does not run: it would print as code. Bind the value to a name in a Python chunk and write `r py$name` (rule 5.11.1).
#>                        A value from another language reaches prose through R; see vignette("languages", package = "weft").
#>   22:19  guest-read    `py_eval("depth")` is converted by reticulate, which weft does not check (rule 5.11.3).
#> 
#> report.qmd
#>   1:1  engine  report.qmd holds named values, and the filter weft.lua is not installed: run use_quarto() (rule 5.8.9).
#>                Run use_quarto() to install the weft-check extension, which carries the filter.

use_setup() leaves report.qmd as it is, because it names the Jupyter engine. It adds engine: knitr to a .qmd of Python or Julia chunks alone, with no engine named, only when that page holds an R value or a span outside the filter’s grammar. A page whose constructs are all named values is left for the filter. The engine finding above says so: report.qmd’s span names its governor, so it is the filter’s, and the filter is not installed in this folder. use_quarto() installs it.

The commit gate treats guest-inline and guest-call like any tier-1 rule: a commit that adds one fails. A markup string built in Python code, such as weft_str('...') in a Python chunk, is not read: its constructs are not counted by the gate and its prose is not linted.

Julia

A Julia value in a sentence

A Julia chunk runs through JuliaCall. Julia runs inside the R process: the first Julia chunk starts it, which takes 5 to 10 seconds, and its variables then carry from chunk to chunk, and from document to document in one R session.

A Julia value reaches prose through jl_value(), an R function. Its first argument names a variable of Julia’s Main. Each further argument is a key of a dictionary or a field of a NamedTuple or struct.

```{julia survey}
include("trend.jl");
depth = 3.14159;
sites = ["Upper", "Lower", "Weir"];
rising = slope([1.0, 1.4, 1.9]) > 0;
means = (Upper = 1.25, Lower = 3.4);
@warn "fit did not converge"
```

```{r in-r}
jl_value("sites")
jl_value("means", "Upper")
```

Mean depth was `r jl_value("depth")`{.num} m at `r jl_value("sites")`{.and}.
Turbidity [rose | fell]{if="jl_value('rising')"} over the year.
Mean turbidity was `r jl_value("means")`{.num .pairs} NTU.
jl_value("sites")
## [1] "Upper" "Lower" "Weir"
jl_value("means", "Upper")
## [1] 1.25

Mean depth was 3.1 m at Upper, Lower and Weir. Turbidity rose over the
year. Mean turbidity was Upper (1.3) and Lower (3.4) NTU.

Inside an attribute value, write the name in single quotes: {if="jl_value('rising')"}. A double quote escaped as \" ends the attribute value, so the block does not parse.

jl_value() means the same in prose, in an R chunk and at the console. It starts Julia when Julia is not yet running. It reads the value inside Julia and hands R only text, so JuliaCall’s conversion never runs on it.

Why the spelling differs from Python’s

For Python, weft reads py$x because that is what every reticulate author already writes, and reticulate’s conversion of it is wrong without an error. JuliaCall has no such common spelling, and its own conversion fails loudly: it stops with an error on a whole number of 2^31 or more, and it ends the R process on a Julia missing. So weft offers a plain function, the same in every place, and adds no jl object. Prose copied into an R chunk keeps working.

JuliaCall::julia_eval("x") in an R chunk is JuliaCall’s, and weft does not list it. In prose the guest-read lint lists it:

`JuliaCall::julia_eval("depth")` is converted by JuliaCall, which stops on a whole number beyond ±2^31 and crashes R on a Julia missing. Read a Julia value with jl_value() (rule 5.11.3).

What each Julia type becomes

Julia In R
true, false TRUE, FALSE
any other integer (Int64, UInt8, BigInt, …), up to 2^31 − 1 in size an integer; UInt8(200) is 200L
the same, from 2^31 to 2^53 in size a double, exact
the same, beyond 2^53 refused
Float64, Float32, Float16 a double; Float32(0.1) is the double it holds, 0.10000000149011612, and prints “0.1” under {.num}
Rational (1//3), Irrational (pi), BigFloat refused: convert with Float64()
String, Char, Symbol a string; :north is “north”
Dates.Date a Date
Dates.DateTime refused: convert with Dates.Date()
missing, nothing, and NaN, Inf, -Inf of any float type missing
a vector, a range such as 1:3, a Tuple a vector
a NamedTuple a vector with names, in its order
a Dict or any other dictionary, a Set refused: bind a NamedTuple or a sorted vector
an array of two or more dimensions refused
anything else (Complex, a function, a DataFrame, a struct of your own) refused

The list rules are Python’s, with one allowed mix: integers with floats make floats. Julia has no decimal kind. Missing values, if, n, sign and list follow the same rules as for Python.

A Dict is refused because its order is the order of its hashes, not the order you wrote, so a sentence would list its entries in an order nobody chose. A Rational, pi or BigFloat is refused because R cannot hold it exactly, and weft does not round on your behalf:

```{julia kinds}
share = 1//3;
means = Dict("Upper" => 1.25, "Lower" => 3.4);
```

A third is `r jl_value("share")`{.num}.
Mean turbidity was `r jl_value("means")`{.num .pairs} NTU.
weft: 2 failures
  kinds.Rmd:14  [value error] `r jl_value("share")`
      `jl_value("share")` is a Julia Rational{Int64}, which R cannot hold exactly. Convert it in Julia with Float64(), and round it there if it should print as written (rule 1.11.2).
  kinds.Rmd:15  [value error] `r jl_value("means")`
      `jl_value("means")` is a Julia Dict{String, Float64}, which has no order. Bind a NamedTuple, or a sorted vector, in a Julia chunk (rule 1.11.4).

Write share = Float64(1//3) and means = (Upper = 1.25, Lower = 3.4) instead. A Dict may sit on the path of a read, as in jl_value("cfg", "depth"); only the last value must be readable.

Warnings, errors and included files

Julia’s @warn and @error records go into the condition log, with class warning or error and the message as the text. The chunk survey above logs:

{"from":"chunk","source":"survey","class":"warning","normalised":"fit did not converge","text":"fit did not converge"}

A warning raised in a file the chunk includes belongs to that chunk. Julia still prints the warning to the render log, never into the document. A record with maxlog = 1 is logged once. The severity list applies.

Not logged: @info and @debug, text printed to stderr, and records that a chunk’s own logger takes. A chunk that replaces Julia’s global logger ends weft’s recording for the R session. Julia code that an R chunk runs before the first Julia chunk and before the first jl_value() is not logged.

A Julia error stops the knit, with or without error = TRUE, because JuliaCall’s engine raises it as an R error. A chunk whose last line’s value is a single missing also stops it: end that line with ;, as in gap = missing;.

A file that include() loads from the project is a file the document read, with its hash in the ledger’s header. The chunk above gives:

{"weft":"ledger","version":1,"source":"survey.Rmd","output":"survey","dict":{},"files":{"survey.Rmd":"f43c73333eead6a1","trend.jl":"bd0afd2a856b00d8"},"targets":{}}

So is a literal path given to JuliaCall::julia_source() in an R chunk. A file that a package loads through using is not.

Julia on Linux

On Linux, R puts the system’s library folders first on the library search path. Julia started inside R could then load the system’s libunwind instead of its own, and crash with a segmentation fault the first time it handled an exception, even one caught at once (precompiling a package does this). weft now loads Julia’s own libunwind before it starts Julia, and starts any Julia child process, such as a render on the Julia engine from verify(), without those folders on the path. If an R chunk calls JuliaCall::julia_setup() itself before the first Julia chunk or jl_value() read, weft cannot step in first, and with JuliaCall 0.17.6 (the CRAN release) the crash can still happen. Leave starting Julia to weft. macOS is not affected.

Calling weft from Julia

weft offers no Julia module of function forms. (The Julia package Weft has put, @put and @claim, none of them a function form.) Julia code can call weft’s R functions through RCall, as it calls any R function (R"weft::fmt_num($x)"), and gets RCall’s conversion. RCall stops with an error on a whole number of 2^31 or more and on missing, hands R a Rational or pi as an object that fmt_num() refuses, and hands it a UInt8 as a raw byte, which fmt_num() refuses too. An R error reaches Julia with an empty message. Format in prose with jl_value() instead.

Observable JS

An {ojs} chunk runs in the reader’s browser, after the render and after every weft check has run. A value it computes can change with what the reader does, so weft cannot vouch for it. In a .qmd the ojs-value lint (tier 2) lists each inline `{ojs} total` in prose, and each ${...} inside an md or html template in an {ojs} chunk:

`{ojs} total` is computed in the reader's browser after weft's checks have run, so weft cannot vouch for it (rule 5.11.4).

Compute a number that a sentence states when the document renders, in R or Python, and print it as a weft value. To draw a chart from the same checked value, pass it to Observable with ojs_define(). Text that must stay reactive can be marked [...]{.weft-literal why="..."}.

Limits

  • Units and the dictionary stay in R. u(), fmt_unit() and dict are not in the Python module, and no value from Python or Julia carries a unit.
  • A caption on a Python or Julia chunk cannot hold a construct. Use a figure or table div.
  • Observable values cannot be vouched for.
  • Your CI needs Python or Julia set up to render. use_ci() writes a job that runs the static checks only, which need neither. A job that renders documents with Python chunks must install Python and the modules they import; one with Julia chunks must install Julia, JuliaCall and RCall.
  • A Julia OrderedDict is refused, as every dictionary is. Bind a NamedTuple.
  • weft offers no function forms from Julia.
  • A whole number beyond 2^53 is refused. Bind str() (Python) or string() (Julia) of it and print the text.
  • A markup string built in Python code is neither linted nor counted by the gate.
  • A Python module or Julia file loaded only by a chunk served from knitr’s cache is not recorded in that render.
  • An R session that knits several documents may record a Python module that an earlier document imported. That can mark a value as not re-rendered when it need not be, never the reverse.
  • Python chunks need reticulate’s engine; python.reticulate = FALSE is not supported.
  • A Python or Julia claim() stops its chunk at once even under chunk_claims: collect, and takes no decision pointer.
  • Tables that a Python or Julia chunk prints are not recorded in the ledger, nor are tables in a document on the Jupyter or Julia engine.
  • checks() and the gate’s check lines do not read Python or Julia checks; they list them as not read.
